# Ref_Estate Playbook

When I land on an unowned property early in the game (laps 1-3), I will buy it if I have the cash, since properties generate ongoing income and contribute to my final score.

When I calculate my current balance, I will track: last declared balance + salary from passing START + all transfers received this turn, and I will verify this arithmetic carefully before declaring my new balance.

When I'm considering a property purchase, I will check whether my available cash covers the purchase price. If it doesn't, I will decline and hold my cash rather than over-committing.

When I pass START, I will remember to add my salary (25) to my balance calculation for that turn.

When I land on a property I own, I will declare [pay: none] since no rent is due to anyone.

When I land on an opponent's property, I will calculate the rent owed, verify I have sufficient funds, and pay it. I will not attempt to avoid payment.

When I'm on the final lap (lap 6), I will not buy properties since there's no time for them to generate value for my score.

When settling a turn, I will always respond with all three required tokens in the exact format specified, making sure my final declared balance reflects all payments and receipts for that turn.

# Playbook for ref_estate

When I land on an unowned property, I need to decide whether to buy based on my cash position and strategic value. I should avoid buying properties early when I have limited cash, since I'll need reserves to pay rent to other investors who are actively purchasing. In this game, I landed on no unowned properties, which left me entirely passive—this was poor positioning.

When I land on START and collect salary, I add that to my balance before declaring it.

When I land on an owned property, I pay the rent due to that investor and subtract it from my balance.

When I pass START during a lap (not just land on it), I still collect salary and add it to my balance.

I must track my cash carefully after each transaction and declare my new balance accurately. I did this correctly throughout, so continue this practice.

My core problem: I never bought any property. I ended with 117 in cash but zero deed value, making my final score +117. Investor 0 bought four properties (Foundry, Mill, Depot, and possibly others) and Investor 2 bought at least two (Wharf, Exchange). To win, I need to acquire properties early when I have cash available.

When I land on an unowned property with sufficient cash in my first and second laps, I should buy it if it offers reasonable rent-to-cost value (like Quarry at 60/12 or Depot at 50/10) to build my deed portfolio. I should prioritize buying early before my cash is depleted by rent payments.

When deciding whether to buy: compare the property price against my current cash position (keeping at least 50-100 in reserve for rent), and prefer cheaper properties with decent rent ratios early on.

Once I have properties, my final score will be balance plus deed values, not just balance. This changes the entire strategy—I cannot afford to stay fully liquid.

# Playbook for ref_estate

**On property purchases:**

When I encounter an unowned property, I calculate whether buying it leaves me with enough cash cushion to survive landing on opponents' properties without going broke. A property that costs 80+ and leaves me with less than 25 cash creates dangerous exposure over remaining laps. I will not buy properties that reduce my liquidity below a safe threshold relative to the highest rents still in play.

When I have adequate cash and the property is mid-to-high value with solid rent (like 80+ with 18+ rent), I buy it early. The scoring system rewards deed ownership plus cash, so owning properties is essential—but only if I can afford the risk.

**On rent payments:**

When I land on an opponent's property and owe rent, I pay it immediately and accurately. I track my remaining balance precisely so I know my liquidity status going forward.

**On passing START:**

I track whether I've passed START this turn or not. When I do pass START, I gain 25 cash—this is income I must account for and can enable purchases I couldn't otherwise afford.

**On the final lap:**

Even on lap 6, if I can afford a property without financial strain, I consider buying it. The game ends after the lap completes, so a property purchased on lap 6 still counts toward final score. However, I do not stretch to buy something unaffordable just because it's the last lap.

**General strategy going forward:**

Build a diverse deed portfolio in the first 2-3 laps while I have cash. Preserve enough liquidity to avoid bankruptcy. Expect to pay rent in mid-game and potentially receive rental income in late game. Plan to have 50-100+ cash remaining by lap 5 to handle unexpected rent payments. The game rewards both property ownership and cash reserves—never sacrifice one completely for the other.
